new_statements.quote: It is generally assumed that the macron indicates a stressed long vowel [...] and the prominent part of a stressed diphthong [...]. In spite of Rysiewicz's objections, some of which will be discussed below, I adhere to this point of view. (p. 300) [...] I think that the available material from the Enchiridion is satisfactorily accounted for by the following LAW: a stressed short vowel lost the ictus to the following syllable. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Altpreussisch with an empty rule field and no existing statements; Kortlandt supplies the placement type (free/lexical stress with mobility, plus a phonemic pitch contrast on stressed long syllables), so it fills rather than contradicts the record. It agrees with the standard doctrine it cites (Berneker 1896: 102ff; Trautmann 1910 §89 p. 185, held by the project in the same folder: 'daß das Pr. den freien Wortakzent gehabt hat'), differing from them only on the mechanism of the double consonant (traditional: stressed short vowel is followed by a double consonant; Kortlandt: the double consonant precedes the stressed vowel).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper is a diachronic accentology study, not a synchronic grammar, but its descriptive premises are explicit: Old Prussian (Enchiridion, 1561) had free, lexically/morphologically determined stress inherited from Balto-Slavic, marked in the text by the macron on a stressed long vowel or the prominent half of a stressed diphthong and, on Kortlandt's hypothesis, by a double consonant before a stressed vowel. Stress is not tied to any fixed syllable: initial (kānxtin, āusins, rānkans), second (gennā, mergūmans), or final (semmē, tennā, twaiā, mukinnā) depending on lexeme and paradigm, with traces of Balto-Slavic mobility (spigsnā/spigsnan, antrā/antrem, laikūt/lāiku). The one Prussian-specific regularity is a historical progressive shift: a stressed short vowel gave up the an earlier reading to the following syllable (not diphthongs; possibly open syllables only), comparable to Dybo's law in Slavic and unlike Saussure's law in Lithuanian, which did not operate in Prussian. Stressed long vowels/diphthongs carried a phonemic pitch contrast (rising from the old broken/acute intonation vs falling per oppositionem); no tonal oppositions in unstressed syllables (p. 305).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the only hint is p. 304, where forms whose macron and double consonant disagree (aūpallai, pergimmans, preipirstans, buttantāws) are suggested to have 'contained two accent frames, cf. Dutch afvállen', i.e. compound-like double prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Hirt's law retractions (wijrs, mūti, mergūmans) and retracted-stress verbs in -int (dīlinai, poswāigstinai, podrūktinai, sātuinei) stand outside the progressive-shift pattern; recent Polish loans (maddla, massi, packai, pogattawint) show the shift, dating it late; several macrons are treated as misprints (aucktimmiskū, pogālbenikan); the accentuation of forms with no macron or double consonant (deiws, deiwas..) is declared unknown (p. 299). Evidence limited to the Enchiridion, negative evidence excluded.
new_statements.identity_note: Kortlandt 1974 confines itself explicitly to the Enchiridion (Abel Will's Third Catechism, 1561, Samlandic variety), 'the only source which allows definite conclusions about the Old Prussian accentual system' (p. 299); it does not describe the Pomesanian dialect of the Elbing Vocabulary or the first two catechisms. Any catalog rule should be tagged as the Enchiridion (Samlandic) variety.

tone_statements.citation: Rinkevičius, Vytautas. 2009. Prūsų kalbos kirčiavimo sistema [The accentuation system of Old Prussian]. Doctoral dissertation (humanities, philology), Vilniaus universitetas. Vilnius. 227 pp. (Summary: Altpreussisches Akzentsystem. Vilnius: Vilniaus universiteto leidykla, 2009.)
tone_statements.quote: The dissertation contains a description of the accentual system of Old Prussian as evidenced by the orthography of Prussian written monuments, particularly that of the Third Catechism (which abounds the most in accentological data). ... the methods of identifying the stressed syllable based on the orthography of the written monuments are outlined. The validity of Saussure-Fortunatov’s and Kortlandt’s laws, which have been postulated in the scholarly literature on Old Prussian, is subjected to a re-evaluation. Then, an analysis of the accentual system is undertaken ... to classify the words by accentual paradigm and to elucidate the role of stress in word-formation.
tone_statements.locator: English summary of the dissertation as given in the Lituanistika record (lituanistika.lt/content/21080)
tone_statements.summary: Free, lexically/morphologically determined mobile word accent with accent paradigms (Baltic type); intonational (acute/circumflex) oppositions on stressed long nuclei discussed in the literature it reviews.

tone_statements.translation: First, the sign ˜ (in various transliterations rendered simply as ¯), which is placed over a long stressed syllable. That this sign marked the stress was shown quite convincingly by F. F. Fortunatov … He also showed that in syllables with Baltic diphthongs and with secondary Prussian diphthongs … by placing this sign over the first or the second part of the diphthong, Prussian marked prosodic phenomena corresponding to the Lithuanian acute (1) and circumflex (2): (1) Pr. pogaũt = Lith. pagáuti; … (2) Pr. acc.pl. ãusins = Lith. acc.pl. ausìs …

tone_statements.quote: Here, it is generally agreed that word stress is indicated by the marking of length on a stressed syllable with a macronlike device: wīrans ‘man, acc. pl.’ : Lith. výrus (with -ij- as an allograph of -ī-). In diphthongs, as Fortunatov (1880, 153 ff.) has shown, the marking of (secondary) moric length indicates not only word stress, but also syllable tone: rānkan ‘hand, acc. sg.’ (Lith. rañką, with Baltic circumflex) : kaūlins ‘bone, acc. pl.’ (Lith. káulus, i.e., Baltic acute). … The circumflex in the Greek forms … clearly has no connection with Old Prussian tone

sources.citation: Kortlandt, Frederik. 2000. The Prussian accent shift. Baltistica 34(2): 193-197. doi:10.15388/baltistica.34.2.493 (journal galley serves only p. 196 as a JPEG)
sources.quote: Defends his progressive accent shift; argues final stress in gannan, rikijai (Zamelius hexameters) and the tāns/tennā/tennan paradigm 'arose as a result of the progressive accent shift'; unstressed vowels shorter than stressed. Presupposes lexically/paradigmatically determined accent place.

sources.quote: Reports Milewski's four OP nominal accent paradigms (barytone and mobile, acute and circumflex) parallel to Lithuanian, and Kortlandt 1974: OP 'shared the common Balto-Slavic accentual innovations and ... differs from the Balto-Slavic base mainly by a single progressive accent shift'; macron marks stressed long vowels; dispute is over double consonants and shifts, not over lexical accent placement.

sources.note: Treats Old Prussian SYLLABLE INTONATION (priegaidė, i.e. the acute vs circumflex tonal contrast on stressed long nuclei): the OPr. suffix -īng- shows circumflex where Lith. -ìng- and Latv. -îg- have acute; explained either by late, independent stressing of the suffix in OP after intonations had been neutralised in unstressed syllables (whereas Lith. stressed it by Saussure-Fortunatov's law while intonations were still distinct in unstressed syllables), or by contraction -īwing- > -īng- (wertīngs: wertīwings). Thus presupposes that OP distinguished acute and circumflex under stress, recoverabl…

tone.quote: The difference in syllable intonation between the circumflex of OPr. -īng- and the acute of Lith. -ìng-, Latv. -îg- could be explained by the fact that these suffixes acquired stress relatively recently in the separate languages. In Lithuanian it became stressed as a result of Saussure-Fortunatov’s law, i.e. in the period when syllable intonations were distinguished in both stressed and unstressed syllables, whereas the stress of OPr. -īng- might be posterior to a possible neutralisation of syllable intonations in unstressed syllables.

sources.citation: Rinkevičius, Vytautas. 2006. Prūsų kalbos pirminių vardažodžių morfemų akcentinė galia [The accentual power of Old Prussian primary nominal morphemes]. Baltistica 41(2): 205-217. doi:10.15388/baltistica.41.2.973
sources.note: First morphological-accentology description of OP: roots and endings are accentually strong or weak; strong-root nouns (grīkai, kaulei, crixtiānimans, rūkai, wijrai; kīrki, kurpi, mūti, rīki, tapali..) have constant stem stress, weak-root nouns (gallū, gennāmans, mensā, mergūmans, widdewū; semmē..) are mobile; strong endings (nom.sg.f. -ā/-ū, -ē; nom.pl.m. -ai; dat.pl. -āmans/-ūmans, -amans) take stress after weak roots, weak endings (acc.sg. -an, -; acc.pl. -ans, -ins..) never do. A stress-placement (an earlier reading) study; intonations not mentioned in the abstract.

tone.quote: The article presents the first attempt to describe the Old Prussian accentuation system based on the main principles of morphological accentology. It aims to distinguish accentual properties of morphemes that determine the placement of stress in primary (non-derived) Old Prussian nouns. ... Thus nouns with strong roots (eg. grīkai, kaulei, crixtiānimans, rūkai ...) belong to the constant stem-stress class, while nouns with weak roots (eg. gallū, gennāmans, mensā, mergūmans, widdewū; semmē ...) belong to the mobile stress class.
